brief: BofA's September jobs report came in soft (NFP 29k, unemployment rate 4.2%) but not surprisingly so, given the punitive seasonal adjustment BofA had anticipated (304k subtracted versus 229k a year earlier, linked to a shorter four-week August survey interval). Private payrolls (46k) landed close to BofA's below-consensus 50k forecast, and the three-month average (50k) stayed above breakeven. The unrounded unemployment rate moved only from 4.14% to 4.17%, with the labor-force participation rate up two-tenths to 61.8%, which BofA calls a benign move for good reasons: household employment rose a robust 406k. Weakness was concentrated in leisure/hospitality and local-government education, while construction and manufacturing held steady on data-center and defense spending. Wage growth slowed to 0.1% m/m from 0.3%, the most dovish element of the report. Though BofA argues this shouldn't shift the Fed's inflation focus, dovish Fedspeak this week led markets to price October hike odds down from 30% to 20%, pulling the implied terminal rate to 4.6% and challenging BofA's own pay-2Y and curve-flattening positioning. BofA says risk has shifted away from its own October hike call and it will revisit that call after the September CPI release, which it expects to matter more for the dollar than this report did.
